description: Having become sole emperor by defeating Licinius in 324, Constantine rebuilt the old Greek city of Byzantium on a grand scale, with a forum, palace, hippodrome, senate house and churches, and dedicated it on 11 May 330. Its site on the Bosporus controlled the passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean and lay close to the threatened Danube and Persian frontiers. Protected by the Theodosian Walls from the 410s, it became the capital of the Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire, which outlived the West by almost a thousand years. It fell to the Ottomans in 1453 and, as Istanbul, is today the largest city in Turkey.

title: King Ezana makes Aksum Christian
summary: Taught by Frumentius, a Syrian Christian later made Aksum's first bishop, King Ezana adopts Christianity; his coins swap crescent and disc for the cross.
description: According to the 4th-century historian Rufinus, Frumentius and his brother were Syrian Christians brought to the Aksumite court as boys after their ship was attacked, and Frumentius became an influential tutor to the young Ezana. He was later consecrated bishop of Aksum by Athanasius of Alexandria, and Ezana converted around the 330s or 340s. Ezana's coins and inscriptions show the shift from traditional gods to the Christian cross, making Aksum one of the first states anywhere to adopt Christianity. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church traces its origins to this conversion.

title: The Huns arrive in Europe
summary: Nomadic Huns from the steppe defeat the Alans and Goths north of the Black Sea, setting off migrations that destabilise the Roman Empire.
description: The Huns' origins are uncertain; a link with the Xiongnu of Mongolia is possible but debated. Around 370–375 they crushed the Alans and the Gothic Greuthungi, and in 376 tens of thousands of Goths sought refuge across the Danube; mistreated by Roman officials, they rebelled and destroyed an eastern Roman army at Adrianople in 378, killing the emperor Valens. Under Attila (r. 434–453) the Huns built an empire centred on the Hungarian plain, extracted huge payments from Constantinople, invaded Gaul in 451, where they were checked at the Catalaunian Plains, and raided Italy in 452. After Attila's death their empire quickly fell apart and had disappeared by about 469.

title: Roman Empire divided between East and West
summary: Theodosius I, the last emperor to rule the whole Roman Empire, dies at Milan, leaving the East to his son Arcadius and the West to Honorius.
description: Theodosius I, a general from Hispania, was made emperor in the East in 379 after the Goths destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378, and he later settled the Goths inside the empire as allies under their own leaders. In 380 his Edict of Thessalonica declared Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire's subjects, and laws of 391–392 banned pagan sacrifice and closed temples. After defeating usurpers in the West he briefly ruled the whole empire, but on his death at Milan in January 395 it passed to his young sons, Arcadius in Constantinople and Honorius in the West. Imperial power had often been shared before, yet this division proved permanent: the wealthier East survived as the Byzantine Empire for more than a thousand years, while the Western empire disintegrated within a century.

title: Austronesian sailors settle Madagascar
summary: Seafarers from Island Southeast Asia cross the Indian Ocean and settle Madagascar, where they later mix with migrants from mainland Africa.
description: The Malagasy language belongs to the Austronesian family and is most closely related to Ma'anyan, spoken in southern Borneo, while Malagasy people have roughly equal Southeast Asian and East African genetic ancestry. Reaching Madagascar meant crossing or skirting some 6,000 km of ocean, probably by way of trade routes around the Indian Ocean rim, making it one of the great prehistoric voyages. Crops such as rice, outrigger canoes and many cultural traditions reflect this Southeast Asian heritage. Genetic studies suggest that the Austronesian and African populations mixed around 1,000 years ago.
mainstreamView: That Austronesian speakers from Island Southeast Asia played a central role in settling Madagascar is well established. When they arrived is debated: some archaeologists argue for scattered, earlier human visits to the island, while firm evidence of permanent village settlement mostly dates from the 7th–8th centuries CE onward, and estimates for the Austronesian arrival range from about the 1st to the 8th century CE.

title: Visigoths sack Rome
summary: Alaric's Visigoths plunder Rome for three days, the first time the city has fallen to a foreign enemy in about 800 years.
description: Alaric's Goths had alternately served and fought the empire for years and repeatedly besieged Rome while seeking land and an official command from the western emperor Honorius, who stayed safely in Ravenna. When negotiations failed, the Visigoths entered Rome on 24 August 410 and plundered it for three days, though they largely spared the churches. Rome was no longer the seat of government, but the shock across the Roman world was immense, and it prompted Augustine of Hippo to write The City of God in defence of Christianity. The Visigoths later settled in south-western Gaul and Spain, founding a kingdom that lasted until 711.

title: Murder of Hypatia
summary: The mathematician and Neoplatonist philosopher Hypatia, a leading teacher in Alexandria, is killed by a Christian mob.
description: Hypatia, daughter of the mathematician Theon, taught philosophy and astronomy to pagans and Christians alike and wrote commentaries on mathematical works such as Diophantus' Arithmetica, none of which survive with certainty. She was an adviser to Orestes, the Roman prefect of Egypt, who was locked in a bitter political feud with the bishop Cyril. In March 415 a mob of Christians led by a lector named Peter seized her, killed her in a church and burned her remains. Later writers made her a symbol of reason destroyed by fanaticism or of the end of classical learning, though historians stress the local political causes of her murder and note that Alexandrian scholarship continued after her death.

title: Ilopango eruption devastates El Salvador
summary: A huge eruption of Ilopango volcano buries Maya settlements across central El Salvador under ash and pyroclastic flows.
description: The Tierra Blanca Joven eruption of Ilopango, now a caldera lake beside San Salvador, was one of the largest in Central America in the last several thousand years. Pyroclastic flows and thick ashfall made much of central and western El Salvador uninhabitable for decades, displacing many thousands of people, and ash fell across a wide area of Mesoamerica. Radiocarbon dating of a tree buried by the eruption, combined with ice-core records, points to a date of about 431 CE, whereas earlier studies had proposed dates ranging from the 3rd to the 6th century, including a link to the climate downturn of 536.

title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: The Germanic general Odoacer deposes the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna, conventionally ending the Western Roman Empire.
description: Through the 5th century the western empire lost Britain, much of Gaul and Spain, and North Africa, where the Vandals took Carthage in 439 before sacking Rome in 455, while real power passed to military strongmen and federated barbarian armies. In 476 Odoacer, leader of the Germanic troops in Italy, deposed Romulus Augustulus, appointed no successor and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, ruling Italy as king. Whether this marked a sudden 'fall' or a gradual transformation into the post-Roman kingdoms of the early Middle Ages is a long-running historical debate. The Eastern Roman Empire, centred on Constantinople, continued until 1453.

title: Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya
summary: Aged 23, the astronomer Aryabhata completes a treatise giving π as 3.1416, a table of sines and the idea that the Earth rotates daily.
description: Written in Sanskrit verse at Kusumapura, usually identified with Pataliputra (Patna), the Aryabhatiya covers arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry and astronomy. It relies on place-value arithmetic, approximates π as 3.1416, gives a table of sines, explains lunar and solar eclipses by the shadows of the Earth and Moon, and proposes that the apparent daily motion of the stars is caused by the Earth's rotation. Indian mathematicians of this era were developing the decimal place-value numerals with a symbol for zero that later reached Europe through the Islamic world as 'Arabic numerals'; the Bakhshali manuscript, partly radiocarbon-dated to the 3rd–4th centuries CE, uses a dot for zero, although that dating is disputed. Aryabhata's work strongly influenced later Indian and Islamic astronomy.
